paragraphs.source_en: As noted earlier, toxic plants were used in the Central Sahara as well. The Uan Afuda cave in the Acacus revealed an accumulation of dung attributed to mouflon (Ammotragus lervia) which was interpreted as keeping and taming mouflon for the slaughter of the animal when food becomes scarce (Cremaschi & Di Lernia 1998: 151; Di Lernia 1999: 222; 231; 237). However, the palynological study of the dung revealed that it contained more than 80% Echium, a toxic plant which may suggest a different interpretation. Such an abundant presence of the narcotic plant in the dung suggests that it was brought into the shelter in a large quantity and given as food to the animals. Why were mouflon fed by a toxic plant? Di Lernia (1999; 2001) argues that the introduction of Echium to mouflon was constant and perfectly conscious.

paragraphs.source_en: Giving toxic plants to mouflon may have had practical reasons but considering their natural docility this hypothesis does not convince. Considering also the predominant position which mouflon, together with the antelope, have in the Round Head art, the intoxication of mouflon for spiritual reasons should be proposed. In the South African rock art, some antelope such as eland are largely predominant and they play a fundamental role in the ideology. We can therefore postulate a similar situation for the Round Head antelope and mouflon. Archaeological evidence from Uan Afuda has been interpreted as the taming of mouflon by Early Holocene hunter-gatherers whose increasing cultural complexity and adaptation to possible environmental stress resulted in the early foodproduction process (Cremaschi & Di Lernia 1996c).

paragraphs.source_en: Considering its great importance in the rock art, I argue that the association of mouflon with a toxic plant at Uan Afuda cave was ritually motivated. The association of eland with narcotic plants during San rituals and rainmaking is ethnographically documented so that there is no reason to exclude this theory for Uan Afuda as well. The cave itself, or just the animals, could have become part of the rituals which are perceptible in the Round Head art.
